qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture thirteen. Thread-level parallelism. How one computer does many jobs at once.
Crumb and Co, a little bakery, must tally a year of receipts every night before seven.
Crumb & Co must tally a year of receipts before 7.
One worker, one slip at a time, is too slow.
One worker, one by one, is too slow.
Parallelism splits the work. It can happen at the level of processes, threads, instructions or data.
Parallelism works at the process, thread, instruction and data level.
This lecture is about threads inside one machine.
This lecture: threads inside one machine.
With processes, each one is a separate program with its own memory.
Process-level: each process has its own memory.
Spawning a new process every time is expensive, like building each baker a kitchen.
Spawning a new process every time is expensive.
With threads, one process starts several threads.
Thread-level: one process starts several threads.
Each runs on its own core, and all share one memory. One kitchen, many cooks.
Each runs on its own core; all share one memory.
This is the model built for multi-core processors.
The model built for multi-core processors.
Machines are sorted by counting streams. S I S D has one instruction stream and one data stream.
SISD: one instruction stream, one data stream.
In S I M D, one instruction, add twenty percent V A T, runs on four processors at once, each on its own price.
SIMD: the same instruction on many processors, each with its own data.
In M I M D, every processor has its own instructions and its own data.
MIMD: each processor has its own instructions and its own data.
Cores running separate threads work this way.
Cores running separate threads work this way.
A thread is a stream of execution spawned by a process.
A thread: a stream of execution spawned by a process.
Threads share memory, such as the global total and the open receipts file.
Threads share memory: global variables and open files.
So every thread sees its parent process data, even one started later.
Every thread can see the parent process's data.
Nothing has to be copied or sent first.
Nothing has to be copied or sent first.
Twelve one-minute blocks on four cores. One thread does all twelve in twelve minutes, while three cores sit idle.
1 thread does all 12 blocks: 12 minutes, 3 cores idle.
Two threads take six blocks each. Six minutes.
2 threads, 6 blocks each: 6 minutes.
Four threads, one per core, take three each. Three minutes, a speed-up of four.
4 threads on 4 cores, 3 blocks each: 3 minutes.
But threads need a shared memory, so they stay on one node. Another computer cannot see it.
Threads need a shared memory, so they stay on one node.
In Open M P, you mark the slow part, and the compiler adds the threads.
OpenMP: mark what to parallelise; the compiler adds the threads.
At a fork, the master thread spawns workers, and each tallies its own share.
Fork: the master thread spawns worker threads.
The faster workers wait for the slowest.
Faster threads wait for the slowest.
The join is a sync point. Then the master carries on alone.
Join: a sync point. Then the master carries on alone.
The night shift runs load, tally, sort, tally, report. On one thread, sixteen minutes.
1 thread: load, tally, sort, tally, report: 16 minutes.
With two threads, each tally is forked and joined. Ten minutes.
2 threads: each tally is forked and joined: 10 minutes.
With four threads, seven minutes.
4 threads: 7 minutes.
But the four sequential minutes never shrink. Only the parallel parts get faster.
The 4 sequential minutes never shrink.
Now three shops run three processes. Each sees only its own data.
Distributed memory: each process sees only its own data.
Process zero sends its total to process two, and process two posts a matching receive. Delivered.
A message needs a send and a matching receive.
If process two waits for process one instead, nothing matches, and the message is not received.
Receive from the wrong sender: no match.
M P I, the Message Passing Interface, is the standard library for this.
MPI is the standard library for this.
The world communicator holds every process, here twelve, ranked zero to eleven.
MPI_COMM_WORLD holds every process: ranks 0 to 11.
Split into groups of three, each group numbers its members zero, one and two.
Split into groups of 3: each numbers its members 0, 1, 2.
So process seven is rank seven in the world, and rank one in group C.
Process 7: rank 7 in the world, rank 1 in group C.
A communicator has a context, a group, a size and ranks counted from zero.
A communicator has a context, a group, a size and ranks.
Threads share one memory, so they split the data on one machine.
The master forks workers and joins them, and only the parallel parts get faster.
Separate processes talk by M P I messages. Next: Workshop thirteen W.
